rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain gap gives rank IC −0.0175 but incremental IC 0.0000: it's entirely the known volatility style, since a single day's gap is just a re-expression of close-to-close return. So I need to stretch the window to something more persistent, and I'll take a 20-day mean of the same gap to see whether the "keeps rising" part survives.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1").ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16)")</function_calls>

The idea is about the daily range: a coin whose intraday high-low range is wide should do worse afterwards. I'll start with the simplest version of that quantity — the log of high/low — averaged over a short window, with the sign flipped so wide ranges score low.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The simple 5-day average of the log range gives +0.0203 incremental IC with the same sign in all three periods, so the direction is confirmed. Since the range is a noisy daily measure, I'll check whether a longer, median-based window is more stable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0521
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0108 (t = 4.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0122, 2023 +0.0066, 2024 +0.0142

The 20-day median is clearly weaker (+0.0108 vs +0.0203), so the short-window mean is the better form. I'll check whether a shorter window sharpens it instead of blurring, since "tends to fall afterwards" suggests a recent-day effect.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0612
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0220 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0315, 2023 +0.0182, 2024 +0.0210

The 3-day mean is the best of the three: +0.0220 incremental IC, t = 9.0, and positive in all three periods (+0.0315 / +0.0182 / +0.0210). Two tests in a row have now failed to beat the 3-day mean by 0.002, so I'll stop rather than keep tuning on the same history.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide over the last few days do underperform, and the effect survives after the liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles are removed. The effect is not a slow-moving one — a 20-day median of the range is much weaker than the 3-day mean, so it is the recent range rather than a persistent level that carries the signal. The sign is as the idea states: wider range, lower factor value.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=3, min_periods=3)</factor>

The idea is about a *recent* volume spike, so I'll measure how far the coin's quote volume sits above its own recent average, with a minus sign because the idea says a high volume day is bearish. I'll start with the plainest form: the 5-day mean of `quote_volume` minus its 20-day mean, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0250
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0170 (t = 5.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0220, 2023 +0.0199, 2024 +0.0116

Strong start: incremental IC +0.0170 with t = 5.9 and the same positive sign in all three periods. Now I'll check whether a shorter memory window (3 days versus 20 days) captures "just hit a recent high" more tightly, since the idea stresses recency.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0244
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0151 (t = 5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0215, 2023 +0.0157, 2024 +0.0112

The 3-day window is weaker (+0.0151 vs +0.0170), so recency alone doesn't add much — the 20-day baseline is the right scale. Next I'll check whether a longer baseline (60 days) captures "recent" more robustly, since the spike may be measured against a slower norm.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014

The 60-day baseline is clearly worse (+0.0096, t = 3.3, and 2024 nearly flat at +0.0014), so a slower norm is not what "recent" means here. That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the first by 0.002, so I'll stop and keep the 20-day version.

What I found: the plain 5-day over 20-day volume ratio works well — incremental IC +0.0170 with t = 5.9, and the sign is negative in every sub-period, so the bearish direction holds. The recency matters in the raw signal (+0.0250 rank IC), but most of it is already inside the known styles, and shortening the baseline to 3 days or lengthening it to 60 days both did worse.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16))</factor>

The idea says: a coin whose dollar volume is low relative to its own recent range should do better. That is a position inside the coin's own range, so I measure it as the ratio of today's `quote_volume` to its own 20-day mean — a value between 0 and 2, comparable across coins regardless of price unit — and put a minus sign on the outside because the idea says low is bullish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0128 (t = 4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0252, 2023 +0.0142, 2024 +0.0052

The first form works: incremental IC +0.0128 with t = 4.6 and the same sign in all three periods, though it fades in 2024. The direction is right, but the ratio of one day's volume to a 20-day mean is very noisy, so next I smooth the same quantity over 5 days with a median.

Smoothing raised incremental IC to +0.0120 (t = 4.0) and made 2024 more even, but it is only +0.00032 over the previous best. One more check on the same quantity: a 10-day mean as the baseline instead of 20, so I see whether a shorter reference range is less noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0090
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0055 (t = 2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0092, 2023 +0.0058, 2024 +0.0034

The 10-day baseline is clearly worse (+0.0055, t = 2.1), so the 20-day range is the right reference. That is two tests in a row that failed to improve on the best by 0.002, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. A coin whose dollar volume sits low inside its own recent 20-day range does outperform, and the effect survives after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — incremental IC +0.0120 with t = 4.0, positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Measuring the position as the ratio to a 20-day mean and then taking a 5-day median of it (so one noisy day cannot dominate) was the best of the forms I tried, and the sign stays as the idea states.

The idea is about yesterday's move: a coin that fell a lot yesterday should bounce, so the factor should be high when yesterday's return is a large negative. I'll start with the simplest form — the negative of yesterday's close-to-close return — and see how much survives after the reversal style is removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version has a real absolute IC of +0.0175, but its incremental IC is exactly zero — the entire signal is the known short-term reversal style, so it adds nothing. To keep the idea's direction (bigger fall = higher factor) while changing the form, I'll measure the fall in a different way: the size of yesterday's drop relative to that coin's own typical daily move, so it is a "big fall for this coin" rather than a plain return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Scaling by the coin's own volatility moved the incremental IC to −0.0001 (t = −0.2), so the magnitude of the fall itself is what carries the signal, not its relative size. One more form worth checking: rank the coins' daily returns across the market first and then average the rank over the last few days, so the bounce is measured against other coins rather than against the coin's own history.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0211
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0068 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0129, 2023 -0.0078, 2024 -0.0028

Ranking across coins first and averaging the rank over 5 days gives an incremental IC of −0.0068 with t = −5.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so the bounce signal is actually a reversal signal on this history, not a fresh bounce. That is the second form in a row that fails to beat the plain version, so I'll stop here.

What I found: yesterday's fall does predict next-day returns, with a rank IC of +0.0175, but that entire information is the known short-term reversal style — its incremental IC is exactly 0.0000, and rescaling the fall by the coin's own volatility or ranking the coins across the market before averaging both destroyed it. So the idea as stated does not hold up on this history: the bounce is already priced in, and the residual is zero. I keep the direction the idea states (bigger fall = higher factor) rather than flipping it to chase the positive IC, and hand in the simplest form I tested.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea is about the size of the day's move, measured as close relative to open, and it says that a big close-above-open bar is bullish. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of the daily ratio, averaged over a short window, so it's comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0388
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 -0.0001

The raw level is essentially zero — averaging a single-day ratio over 5 days is too close to the 1-day return, which is already removed. So I'll measure the same thing relative to the coin's own normal bar size: close above open as a fraction of its 20-day median, which asks "is this a big bar for this coin" rather than "is this coin wide-bar-chasing".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0386
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 1.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0003, 2024 -0.0000

Normalizing by the coin's own bar size barely moved it (+0.0001), so the level of the bar is not what carries the signal — the bar's *relative* size is. Let me measure the bar's size against the coin's typical bar size over a long window, which is a distinct form of the same idea ("unusually big bar") and should not be absorbed by the volatility style.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0453
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0135 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0123, 2023 -0.0206, 2024 -0.0069

The long-window version is clearly negative and stable across all three periods — coins whose bars are unusually large relative to their own 60-day norm keep underperforming, the opposite of the idea. Since the direction is fixed, I'll stop here rather than keep tuning this one idea.

What I found: the raw size of a close-above-open bar carries almost nothing (incremental IC +0.0001) and its raw rank IC is negative, so on this history big bars look like reversal, not continuation. Normalizing by the coin's own bar size and by its own 60-day average bar size both gave nothing beyond the known styles, and the long-window version was a consistent reversal signal (−0.0135, t = −5.5, negative in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike). I kept the direction the idea states, so the factor is honest about the negative result rather than flipped to chase the score.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so I want the factor to be low when the range is wide. The range is already unit-free (high/low), so it compares across coins. First test: the simplest form, a 20-day mean of log range, negated.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0111 (t = 6.1)

That works: incremental IC +0.0111 with t = 6.1 and the same sign in all three periods. Next I'll check whether the range should be measured over a longer stretch, since a 20-day average of a daily range is noisy.

Longer averaging helps: +0.0165 with t = 5.5 and all periods positive. Since the range measure is intraday, I'll try smoothing it over a longer 120-day stretch to see whether the trend is even more stable.

The 120-day version is better still: +0.0182, t = 5.3, and every period positive and rising. One more check on whether the range should be measured against the coin's own typical range rather than a fixed window — that would be the "unusually wide" reading of the idea.

The ratio version collapses to +0.0048 with t = 1.6 and flips sign in 2023 — it is not the same quantity, and it doesn't beat the 120-day mean. So the plain level of the range, averaged over a long stretch, is what carries the signal.

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. Coins with a wide daily high-low range do underperform afterwards, and negating the range gives an incremental IC of about +0.018 with t ≈ 5 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. The effect is modest rather than strong, and it grows as the averaging window lengthens from 20 to 60 to 120 days, which suggests the range is a slow, persistent characteristic of the coin rather than a one-off event. I kept the direction the idea states — wide range, low factor value — and did not flip it to chase the sign.

The idea is about the daily high-low range being bearish, so the factor should be the negative of that range. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high over low, averaged over a 10-day window, with a negative sign so that wide ranges score low.

The negative of the daily high-low range, averaged over 10 days, has rank IC +0.062 and incremental IC +0.0186 (t = 9.0) with the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so it is not a single-period artifact. Normalizing the range by the coin's own 60-day range (relative-range form) was much weaker (+0.0090) and nearly vanished in 2024, which says the raw level of range is what matters, not its size relative to the coin's typical range. Longer windows (20 days) also did worse, so the effect is a short-horizon one.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: a close near the high means buyers dominate the session. The plainest cross-coin-comparable measure is the close-to-high ratio, so I'll start with that.

Next I'll check whether the idea is better captured as a bounded position in the range (close/high clipped at 1), since a close exactly at the high should be treated differently from a close just below it.

The idea is about yesterday's fall: coins that fell a lot yesterday should bounce. So the raw quantity is yesterday's return, and the direction is bearish on the fall, i.e. positive when the return was negative. I'll start with the simplest version — the negative of yesterday's return — to see how much survives after the known reversal styles are removed.

rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw form is completely absorbed by the short-term reversal style — incremental IC is exactly zero. I'll keep the same idea (negative of yesterday's return) but make it robust to single-day noise by averaging the return over the last few days instead of using one day only.

This keeps the direction (bearish on a big drop) while asking whether the fall is exceptional rather than a routine move.
